reader_rows.why_it_matters: A commercial pipeline already carries a per-level end-plate width prior in mm and shows widths vary little enough across levels to scale a film, which is exactly why a width alone names a level poorly.

reader_rows.name: SpineCAMP versus QMA and QMA's own validation
reader_rows.row_markdown: | SpineCAMP (fully automatic) versus QMA analysts on flexion-extension films, NASSJ 2026 [full]; QMA's truth Zhao 2005 and Pearson 2011 [abstract] | Not public, 120 lateral films from 49 sites, 66 cervical and 59 lumbar levels after 4 excluded; QMA analysts as the reference; QMA itself was validated on six cadaver lumbar spines against electromagnetic sensors (Zhao 2005, J Biomech 38:1943) and on 30 flexion-extension sets by three observers twice (Pearson 2011, Spine 36:572) | No (Medical Metrics, FDA-cleared; employees and stockholders among the authors) | Rotation MAE 0.16 and 0.18 degrees, translation MAE 0.09 and 0.14 mm, ICC 0.98 to 1.00, four body corners per vertebra; QMA rotation error 0.47 +/- 0.24 degrees against sensors (surgeons 2.16 +/- 0.78), the "0.54 mm" the 2026 paper quotes is not in Zhao's abstract; Pearson gives ICCs only (rotation 0.997, translation 0.959 intra-observer) | Motion, not morphometry: no end-plate width or line output, no mm error of a corner position published, levels from the pipeline's own labelling |
reader_rows.where_in_note: Section 2.1 "End-plate inclination and wedge angle" after the bullet on Hipp's later automated metrics; section 3 table after the Hipp 2022 row (or merged into it)
reader_rows.why_it_matters: Answers the Gaps question: Spine Camp's QMA validation is published with degree figures on cadavers and ICCs, but no corner or end-plate landmark error in mm.

reader_rows.name: Vrtovec vertebral inclination studies
reader_rows.row_markdown: | Vrtovec 2011, 2013, 2014 vertebral inclination by symmetry planes, CT and MRI (Spine 36:E875; Clin Radiol 68:807; CMIG 38:620) [abstract] | Not public, 28 vertebrae T4 to L5 in CT, in coronal MRI, and in sagittal MRI of one normal and one scoliotic subject; three observers, two occasions, six manual line methods | No | Coronal MRI: manual mid-end-plate lines the most reproducible (1.0 degree intra- and 1.4 inter-observer SD), computerised 3D symmetry 0.8 and 1.3; sagittal CT: mid-wall lines 1.0 and 1.4, computerised 0.9 and 1.3; sagittal MRI: superior and inferior tangents 2.6 to 4.5 degrees SD and computerised 3D 3.1 and 5.2, so the authors conclude inclination should follow the body walls | One inclination per vertebra, not a superior and inferior slope; 28 vertebrae; no mm, no level naming |
reader_rows.where_in_note: Section 2.1 "End-plate inclination and wedge angle" after the Cina 2021 bullet; section 3 table after the Cina 2021 row
reader_rows.why_it_matters: Gives the observer floor for an end-plate tangent, about 1 degree SD on CT and 2.6 to 4.5 on sagittal MRI, which brackets whether a 2 to 5 degree Panjabi inclination is readable at all.

reader_rows.name: Six-point morphometry software outputs (SpineAnalyzer, Hologic MXA, GE Lunar DVA)
reader_rows.row_markdown: | Six-point morphometry software: SpineAnalyzer (K103475), Hologic MXA (patent US5483960) and GE Lunar DVA (K023554) [page]; SpineAnalyzer on Rotterdam films [full, QIMS]; Hologic VFA readers [abstract] | No end-plate truth: SpineAnalyzer validated on Rotterdam Study lateral films T4 to L4 against manual Cobb only (n 99); Hologic six-point VFA on 96 images by three radiographers | No (commercial); SpineAnalyzer's 510(k) carries no performance data, GE DVA "bench testing only" | Outputs are anterior, middle and posterior heights (SpineAnalyzer's in pixels), wedge Ha/Hp, biconcavity Hm/Hp and crush ratios and Genant grades; Hologic's report lists AH, MH, PH in mm and WEDGE and MWEDGE ratios; GE DVA is a visual image that estimates vertebral heights; Hologic six-point heights ICC 0.96 between readers; SpineAnalyzer's 95-point contour is suggested but "not ... validated" | None outputs an end-plate width, depth, area or inclination; T4 to L4; levels named by the analyst's centre clicks (13 points T4 to L4 in SpineAnalyzer) |
reader_rows.where_in_note: Section 3 table after the TPTBox row, with one sentence in section 2.3 after the public-code paragraph
reader_rows.why_it_matters: Closes the Gaps item on DXA morphometry: the six points would allow an end-plate width but no software reports one, so no DXA reference table of end-plate widths exists.

reader_facts.row: Doerr 2020 EndSeg and SpNorm, CT [abstract]
reader_facts.fact: Dataset: 7 patient CTs from SpineWeb Dataset 14 (Munoz 2013), C7 to S1, with normal or abnormal kyphosis and lordosis and no significant scoliosis; input is the CT plus one point label per vertebra placed by a radiologist. Truth: five readers (two radiologists, three spinal neurosurgeons) marking one end-plate per DRR on 128 DRRs; inter-reader CI95 8.2 degrees proximal thoracic kyphosis, 6.0 main thoracic, 7.4 lumbar lordosis, 11.0, 8.2 and 4.8 coronal, mean inter-reader error 7.6. End-plate angle = slope of a line fitted to the segmented end-plate's projection. Table 5 mean difference against manual at T2, T3, T4, T8, L1, L3, S1: EndSeg -3.6, -4.0, -2.2, 0.1, 0.4, 1.9, 0.8 degrees, average absolute difference 1.9 (paired t p = 0.33); SpNorm -2.1, -1.6, -0.4, 1.4, 2.6, 5.6, -5.3, average 2.7 (p = 0.83). 93.8 percent of both methods' end-plate angles inside the inter-reader CI95; alignment metrics mostly within 3.0 degrees, thoracic kyphosis up to about 6; region growing stable above tau about 5 degrees with error about 0.5 degree. No Dice or mm for the end-plate segmentation, no runtime, no code or data statement. Row cells become: 7 SpineWeb CTs, five readers; code not stated; average absolute end-plate angle difference 1.9 degrees (EndSeg) over seven levels, readers' CI95 6 to 8 degrees.

reader_facts.row: Kishimoto 2016 3D end-plate meshes, CT [abstract]
reader_facts.fact: 49 patients (25 men, 24 women), 22 to 88 years, mean 61.8, lumbar canal stenosis 27, disc herniation 14, cervical disorders 6, two other; whole-spine myelography CT at 1.0 mm slices, pixel 0.39 +/- 0.07 mm. Mimics 16.0 at a 226 HU threshold with the Wrap function at 1.0 mm; end-plates were "further segmented from each vertebral 3D model" with no statement whether by hand; manifest osteophytes left out; 2,352 end-plate models from 1,176 bodies C2 to S1; areas by a custom Visual C++ routine. No intra- or inter-observer reliability anywhere. Table 1 superior polygon area, men, C3 to S1: 307.7, 376.9, 394.9, 469.0, 465.0, 441.3, 458.4, 467.0, 509.9, 552.4, 603.8, 675.4, 772.8, 842.4, 919.9, 1047.2, 1178.2, 1280.1, 1447.3, 1582.4, 1581.9, 1579.1, 1505.4 mm2 (women 265.0 at C3 to 1357.7 at L5 and 1303.4 at S1); inferior, men, 314.9 at C2 to 1699.8 at L4 and 1560.7 at L5; polygon over projected area 1.06 +/- 0.05. Position is the cumulative centroid distance from C2 as a percentage of C2 to S1; r 0.938 (men) and 0.911 (women) polygon, 0.943 and 0.922 projected, no equation printed. The T4 dip is in transverse diameter, not area; area falls L4 to L5 (inferior, both sexes) and L5 to S1 (superior). Table 2 gives AP and transverse diameters per level (C3 superior men 14.3 and 20.7 mm, L5 34.0 and 52.8). Row cells become: no reliability at all; thresholded Mimics meshes, manual steps unstated.

reader_facts.row: Chen 2013 manual cervical end-plates, CT [abstract]
reader_facts.fact: 97 PACS patients scanned for head and neck symptoms with no spinal complaint, mean age 41 (25 to 51), four age-sex groups of 22, 26, 28 and 21; exclusions for osteophytes, degeneration, fracture, tumour, rotation or slant; GE LightSpeed VCT at 0.625 mm, midsagittal reformat chosen at the full spinous process contour; manual with the PACS tools by one trained user, repeats not stated, no reliability statistic; precision 0.3 mm for depth and 1.5 degrees for slope, which explains printed SDs of 0.0. Definitions: depth = perpendicular from the apex to the line joining the anterior and posterior rims; apex location = anterior rim to apex over that line's length; slope = 90 degrees minus the angle between the rim line and the anterior wall. 970 end-plates: superior depth 1.2, 0.9, 0.9, 1.2, 1.2 mm and inferior 2.4, 2.7, 2.1, 2.4, 2.1 at C3 to C7; superior slope 7.5, 7.5, 9.0, 7.5, 4.5 degrees and inferior 7.5, 7.5, 7.5, 7.5, 4.5; apex 56 to 67 percent superior and 52 to 57 inferior. Row cells become: one reader, no reliability; the slope is relative to the anterior wall, not to the other end-plate.

reader_facts.row: Feng 2019 scanner point clouds [abstract]
reader_facts.fact: Nothing beyond the abstract could be read (JoVE's page empty twice, not in PMC): the abstract confirms a high-speed scanner's point cloud, a 3D coordinate system, three sagittal and three frontal curves of 11 equidistant points and fitted parametric equations, with no specimen count, levels, scanner accuracy or reliability; Shanghai East Hospital, Tongji. Row stays as it is.

reader_facts.row: Cappetti 2025 (section 2.1 bullet, [page])
reader_facts.fact: Abstract read through DOAJ's API (DOI 10.1016/j.cmpbup.2024.100175, CMPB Update 7:100175, licence CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 per Crossref): a local coordinate system and rules measure the vertebral body, foramen and spinous process in the sagittal and coronal planes of a high-density point cloud from CT or 3D scanning, automating the radiologists' manual protocol; tested on nine complete cervical tracts against manual measurement, whose intra- and inter-operator ranges were wide, while the method's were consistent; no number, no end-plate dimension named, and the authors call for further validation. Crossref lists the group's earlier Di Angelo 2015 CMPB paper (doi 10.1016/j.cmpb.2015.04.003) and a 2021 CMBBE Imaging and Visualization paper on automatic 3D vertebral features [search]. Tag rises from [page] to [abstract]; which end-plate dimensions and the errors stay unread.

reader_facts.row: The lumbar MR deformity framework (section 2.1 bullet, [page])
reader_facts.fact: The paper is Al-Haidri, Akhatov, Usmanova, Salimov, Al-Habeeb, Il'yasov, Brui, "Deep learning-assisted framework for automation of lumbar vertebral body segmentation, measurement, and deformity detection in MR images", Biomedical Signal Processing and Control 106:107770, August 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.bspc.2025.107770 (Crossref and Semantic Scholar records, neither with an abstract); the 200 subjects, 0.78 to 0.86 mm median heights and 3.3 percent wedge remain from the search summary only.

reader_facts.row: Jang 2023 (section 2.2 BUU-LSPINE bullet, [abstract])
reader_facts.fact: The 1,000 pairs are not BUU-LSPINE: they come from Catholic Kwandong University International St. Mary's Hospital, Incheon, February 2014 to May 2019, 1,000 of 2,000 patients aged 18 to 80 after exclusions; four approximate corners per body L1 to L5 (20 points a view, no S1), the upper and lower pairs joined as end-plate lines; 12 raters in two groups of six with 200 common cases; 1953 x 3000 pixels, 0.143 mm a pixel; errors are distances from the raters' mean, 1.197 to 1.670 mm lateral and 1.469 to 3.430 mm AP (Table 2); end-plate angle RMSE 0.906 to 1.486 degrees lateral, 0.577 to 0.979 AP (Table 4); data "available from the corresponding author on reasonable request", no repository, no licence; the supplementary zip holds x and y breakdowns.

reader_facts.row: Hipp 2022 Spine Camp on NHANES II [full] (the "previously validated" QMA landmarking)
reader_facts.fact: The QMA validation behind Spine Camp is Zhao 2005 (J Biomech 38(9):1943): six cadaveric lumbar spines L1 to S1 with electromagnetic sensors on L3 to L5, lateral films in neutral, flexion and extension, software rotation error 0.47 +/- 0.24 degrees against three surgeons' 2.16 +/- 0.78; Pearson 2011 (Spine 36(7):572) adds ICCs on 30 flexion-extension sets (QMA intra-observer rotation 0.997, translation 0.959, disc height change 0.951 to 0.962). NASSJ 2026 (PMC13579288) quotes QMA as "0.47 degrees and 0.54 mm" citing Zhao; no landmark position error in mm is published in any of them, so the Hipp row's "no landmark mm or degree error" stands.

reader_facts.row: Kramer 2024 mesh landmarks [full] and the Spine-Morphology-Analyzer code
reader_facts.fact: No LICENSE, LICENSE.md or LICENSE.txt on main or master (all 404) and GitHub shows none; 16 commits, 5 stars, default main; root holds SampleData, SlicerPlugins, dataset, datasets, .gitmodules and SpineLib pinned at 773b590 (Caetox/SpineLib, also vendored under SlicerPlugins/SymmetryPlane/SpineLib). SlicerPlugins/Dimensions/Dimensions.py is a 3D Slicer module by Vinzent Rittel (acknowledging Bauer and Kramer) whose help text says it "calculates the endplate slope"; its result table has columns Upper Width, Upper Depth, Lower Width, Lower Depth, Height and four heights at the ends of the sagittal and frontal curves, and its save button writes inter-vertebral angles to CSV, computed in Resources/Scripts/morphology.py as the angle about the right axis between the upper end-plate regression lines of adjacent vertebrae (Vertebra.angle), end-plates taken as faces within max_angle of the up vector. SpineLib (100 commits, no licence, readme of two install lines): VertebralBody.py clips the anterior half, keeps faces whose normals lie within max_angle (45 degrees default in Vertebra.py) of plus or minus the up vector, keeps the largest connected region, cuts a sagittal and a frontal curve through each end-plate and takes their end points as four landmarks per end-plate; Vertebra.py derives width, depth and height from those landmarks; EvaluationTools.py gives mean, SD and RMSE of scalar and point differences and pyvista surface distances; requirements scipy, vtk, open3d, pyvista, pyacvd, scikit-spatial. Row's code cell becomes: Slicer plugin plus SpineLib, both unlicensed, width and depth of both end-plates and an inter-vertebral angle, no inclination per end-plate and no area.

reader_facts.row: vertebral-heights, TotalSegmentator masks [code]
reader_facts.fact: No licence file (404 on main and master, none shown on GitHub); 1 commit, 0 stars, default main; root holds tests/, vertheight/, conftest.py, requirements.txt, vh.cmd; outputs Ha, Hc, Hp, wedge index, biconcavity index, wedge angle, end-plate inlier fractions, symmetry Dice, orientation and a JSON record; no end-plate width or depth; 197 tests on synthetic geometry, phantoms only, 2.0 mm slices uncharacterised. Row unchanged in substance.

reader_facts.row: TPTBox [code]
reader_facts.fact: LICENSE file is Apache-2.0. TPTBox/spine/spinestats holds angles.py, curvature.py, pelvic_parameters.py, measure_ivd_and_vertebra_geometry.py, vertebra_anatomical_widths.py, body_quadrants.py, torso_vat_sat.py and poi_fun/. End-plate functions: compute_segmental_endplate_angles gives the signed sagittal angle between the inferior end-plate directions of adjacent vertebrae (the disc wedge), the end-plate centre from the Endplate subregion or the corpus plus inferior direction; vert_geometry gives per body x1 anterior and x2 posterior heights, x3 and x4 lateral heights, x5 lateral and x6 sagittal width, sagittal_wedge_deg = atan((x1 - x2)/x6), coronal_wedge_deg and wedge indices with a Genant screen below -0.4; vertebra_width_LR_center_mm (between muscle-insert landmarks) and vertebra_width_AP_center_mm (posterior to anterior central median points). No end-plate width, depth, area, per-end-plate inclination or concavity; widths are body widths at the centre; sacral slope uses an S1 end-plate reconstructed from two landmarks; no accuracy against readers in the docs or source read. Row's accuracy cell stays none; lacks cell becomes: wedge angle per vertebra and body widths only, no end-plate measure.

reader_facts.row: Endplate3D-QCT 2025 segmentation benchmark [full]
reader_facts.fact: end_plate_postproc holds evaluate.py (resamples to 1 mm, Dice, Jaccard, HD95 and ASD through medpy, instances matched by Dice with a true positive above 0.8, precision and recall, global Dice and Jaccard), collect_info.py, collect_BMD.py (mean HU inside each end-plate mask L1 to S1, S1 whole), tsv2latex.py, latex.tex, three sample NIfTIs and folders scores_easy, scores_hard, scores_inner and combine_endplate_spine; paths are absolute to the authors' server; no LICENSE at the root or in the folder (404), 5 commits, 1 star, default main. No geometric measure is computed anywhere, so the row's "masks, no measures" stands and the code cell becomes: evaluation code public, unlicensed, segmentation metrics and BMD only.

rows.name: Gupta 2018, the 510-vertebra facet study (facets target 2)
rows.reason: Table gives L3 L 28.6 < R 28.8; gradual T10-L1 3.33 percent too. https://www.aimdrjournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/AT6_OA_Rimpi-edit.pdf
rows.row_markdown: | Gupta, Singla, Agnihotri, Budhiraja, Goyal, Bansal 2018, Ann Int Med Dent Res 4(4):AT29-AT33, doi 10.21276/aimdr.2018.4.4.at6, CC BY-NC [full, journal PDF read by pdftotext] | No digital set. 30 adult male dry thoracolumbar columns (GMC Amritsar), boiled and labelled T1 to L5: 510 vertebrae (360 thoracic, 150 lumbar); the sagittal angle of the superior articular facet by a protractor, a steel wire in the midsagittal plane and a bent hairpin (Patel and Singel 2003) | No | Means only, no repeat or observer figure: thoracic 112 to 120 deg (T1 R 112.5, L 114.0; T6 L 120.3), T12 R 85, L 92.1 (ranges 30-125, 36-134), L1 R 32, L 34.2, L2 29, 29.8, L3 28.8, 28.6, L4 34.1, 32.1, L5 36.9, 40.4; the text says left larger by 0.2 to 7 deg at every level but L4, not significant, though its table has L3 left smaller too and T12 left larger by 7.1; T12 under 90 deg in 14 columns (46 percent) right and 9 (30) left; the change gradual over T11-L1 in 46 percent right and 30 left, over T10-L1 in 3.33, abrupt at T12-L1 in the rest; its Table 1 sets Pal 2000 (reference 9, dated 2001 in its list) and Patel 2004 (Indian, C3 to S1) beside it, their T1 to T3 means identical | 30 men, dry bone, no images, no age or sex analysis, no cervical, one protractor angle per facet, no transitional vertebra; the abstract's "almost equal number" is about 49 gradual against 51 abrupt on the right but 33 against 67 on the left (46 and 30 over T11-L1 plus 3.33 over T10-L1) |

rows.name: Singer 1988 and 1989, CT facet orientation at the thoracolumbar junction
rows.reason: Abstracts never say mortice; 1989 gradual totals 71.5. PubMed 3145570, 23915998 via eutils efetch
rows.row_markdown: | Singer, Breidahl, Day 1988, Surg Radiol Anat 10(4):291-295 (PMID 3145570) and 1989, Clin Biomech 4(2):80-86 (PMID 23915998) [abstract, both] | No. 1988: 214 (176 abdominal CTs, 9 thoracolumbar junction referrals, 29 cadaveric columns), scans through the superior end-plates of T11 to L2, joint angles by a computer-aided digitiser; 1989: 630 people aged 10 to 93 (551 abdominal scans, 26 junction scans, 53 cadaveric spines), joints T10-11 to L1-2 | No | 1988: coronal superior and sagittal inferior processes at T12 in 29 percent, T11 16, L1 0.5; gradual transition 54 percent; tropism over 20 deg at T11-12 21 percent, T12-L1 9. 1989: gradual over three levels (T10-11 to T12-L1) 59.6 percent; progressive T11-12 to L1-2 11.4, T9-10 to T11-12 0.5 (71.5 gradual in all); abrupt at T11-12 to T12-L1 18.1, T10-11 to T11-12 10.2, T12-L1 to L1-2 0.2; asymmetry over 10 deg at T11-12 40.8 percent, T12-L1 17.7; L1 transverse process ossification anomalies 2.06 percent | The largest CT facet-orientation series at the junction found here (630, cadaveric spines among them); four levels, no per-level means in the abstracts, no data, no inter-observer figure, 1980s scanners; the transition lies anywhere from T10-11 to L1-2, so a rule reading T12 from the facet angle meets that spread |

rows.name: Du Plessis 2022, superior facet angle T11 to L1 and the transitional vertebra on CT
rows.reason: Methods say two observers, Results three; 'most scans end there' not found. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9119610/
rows.row_markdown: | Du Plessis and others 2022, J Anat 240(6):1179-1186, doi 10.1111/joa.13619 [full, PMC9119610] | Not open (the paper says the data would be on the University of Pretoria library website in 2022; not checked). 173 adults in the abstract, 175 in the Methods, aged 18 to 80, archived CTs, Windhoek, Namibia, 2018 to 2020; T11, T12, L1 and thoracolumbar transitional vertebrae only; the superior articular facet angle on axial CT in Syngo, reflex angles computed by hand | No | Means T11 184.5 +/- 8.16 deg, T12 182.8 +/- 10.4 (table SD 10.31), L1 112.3 +/- 7.27, TLTV 136 +/- 23.18 (table SD 21.77); left and right not different at normal levels (p 0.10 to 0.246), the TLTV facets asymmetric (mean difference 36.5 +/- 13.08 deg); inter-observer r 0.978 to 0.997 on 10 repeated measurements (three observers in the Results, two in the Methods); 13 or 14 TLTV (the text disagrees), each with another anomaly (hypoplastic ribs 8, spina bifida 5, sacralisation 4, lumbar numeric variation 6, compression fractures 4) | Three levels, one plane, by hand, no abrupt-or-gradual count of its own (it quotes Forseen 2015's 227 of 244 abrupt); the TLTV angle lies between T12's and L1's with two to three times their spread, the facet signature of the one vertebra a rule must not name wrong |

rows.name: Forseen 2015, the facet transition as a way of naming T12 on 244 CTs
rows.reason: Rib denominators 7+11+234=252 vs 244; segment origin unstated. https://api.openalex.org/works/https://doi.org/10.4172/2165-7939.1000222
rows.row_markdown: | Forseen, Bruce, Gilbert, Patel, Ramirez, Borden 2015, J Spine 4(2):222 (OMICS), doi 10.4172/2165-7939.1000222, CC BY [abstract, OpenAlex record; authors from Semantic Scholar] | No. 244 whole-spine CTs; the facet transition (flat posterolateral to curved posteromedial facets), its type (gradual or abrupt), the lowest rib-bearing segment and lumbosacral transitional anatomy read per patient; where segment 1 lies is not stated in the abstract (the lowest rib at the 19th in 92 percent implies C1 is segment 1) | No | Transition abrupt in 227 of 244 (93 percent); the transition at the 19th segment in 184 (75 percent), the 18th in 50 (20), the 20th in 10 (4); the lowest rib set at the 19th in 225 (92), the 20th 11 (5), the 18th 8 (3); lowest full disc 24-25 in 216 (88), 23-24 in 9 (4), 25-26 in 19 (8); lumbosacral transitional anatomy with eleven ribs in 5 of 7, thirteen 8 of 11, twelve 24 of 234 (10 percent), denominators that sum to 252 against 244 and disagree with the 8 and 225 above | The one study found that tests a facet feature as a T12 marker, and it concludes the transition is not reliable and that numbering must count caudally from C2; manual, no angle in degrees, no inter-reader figure, its rib counts internally inconsistent, an OMICS journal |

rows.name: Pal and Routal 1999, abrupt versus gradual on 44 dry columns
rows.reason: Singer 1989 is 71.5 percent gradual, same direction, not reverse. PubMed 10529057, 23915998
rows.row_markdown: - Pal and Routal 1999, J Anat 195(2):199-209, PMID 10529057 [abstract, PubMed]: 44 dry adult columns, T9 to L5; the change of articular process orientation at the thoracolumbar junction abrupt in 3 columns (7 percent) and gradual over 2 or 3 successive vertebrae in 41 (93 percent), the reverse of Forseen 2015's 93 percent abrupt on CT and more gradual than Singer 1989's 71.5 percent (59.6 over T10-11 to T12-L1, 11.4 over T11-12 to L1-2, 0.5 over T9-10 to T11-12) on 630 CT-imaged spines, so the abrupt-or-gradual share depends on the definition and the material and a rule cannot take one share from the literature.

rows.name: Jankowski 2026, the L3 transverse process length as a level landmark across counting variants
rows.reason: Castellvi exclusion applied only to the C7T12L5 reference pool. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13703058/
rows.row_markdown: Jankowski and others, "Reliability of the L3 Transverse Process as a Landmark for Lumbar Spine Enumeration Across Different Vertebral Segmentation Patterns", Diagnostics 2026;16(20):3409, doi 10.3390/diagnostics16203409 (PMC13703058, CC BY) [full] | On request only (ethical and privacy restrictions). 499 polytrauma whole-body CTs of one Polish tertiary hospital, 2022 to 2024, with confirmed numbering; all 49 non-standard formulas (C7T11L5 4, C7T11L6 6, C7T12L4 8, C7T12L6 18, C7T13L4 3, C7T13L5 10) and the 17 C7T12L5 spines left after excluding Jenkins, Castellvi, cervical, thoracolumbar and sacral anomalies, 66 in all; read by two final-year students, reviewed by a neurosurgeon, every case re-measured by a neurosurgeon blind to the first | None (manual multiplanar measurement) | Bilateral lumbar transverse process lengths from the pedicle-lamina junction to the tip; L3 the longest in 45 of 66 (68.2 percent) by single process and 49 of 66 (74.2) by bilateral mean; by thoracic pattern 30.0 / 30.0 (C7T11), 76.7 / 83.7 (C7T12), 69.2 / 76.9 (C7T13), only the bilateral association holding after Holm correction (adjusted p 0.014; single 0.058); the 22nd presacral vertebra longest in 44 of 66 (66.7); inter-reader ICC 0.88 (0.85 to 0.91) for single-side lengths, 0.93 (0.90 to 0.94) for bilateral means | The one study found that scores a posterior-element measure (transverse_length) as a level cue across 11, 12 and 13 rib-bearing patterns, by hand; by single process L3 is not the longest in 23.3 percent of twelve-rib spines (11.8 percent of the 17 typical C7T12L5) and 70 percent of eleven-rib spines; no automation, an enriched sample whose shares are not prevalences, the Castellvi exclusion applied to the reference group only, CT only

rows.row_markdown: SLIDE, Hetherington and others (Int J Comput Assist Radiol Surg 2017;12(7):1189-1198, doi 10.1007/s11548-017-1575-8, PMID 28361323; Can J Anaesth 2022;69(10):1211-1219, doi 10.1007/s12630-022-02300-6, PMID 35941333) and Pesteie and others (IEEE Trans Med Imaging 2018;37(1):81-92, doi 10.1109/tmi.2017.2739110, PMID 28809679; Int J CARS 2015;10(6):901-912, PMID 26026697) [abstract, all four] | Not public; SLIDE is proprietary software. 2017: transverse lower-spine ultrasound classified as sacrum, intervertebral gap or vertebral bone, training size not in the abstract, 20 test scans; 2022: 76 term parturients, the reference an experienced operator's traditional ultrasound (NCT02982317); 2018: expert sonographer annotations, counts not in the abstract; 2015: 1,090 epidural and 1,052 facet-joint images | None stated | 2017: a transfer-learned CNN and a state machine naming the level as the transducer moves up the spine, 88 percent (20-fold cross-validation), 17 of 20 test scans with every level right, 40 frames a second; 2022: agreement with the reference for L3-4 84 percent (Gwet AC1 0.82) against palpation 70 (0.59), adjusted odds ratio 2.99 for L3-4 and all other interspaces after BMI; 2018: epidural target error 1 mm lateral and 0.4 mm vertical on 3-D planes, 1.7 and 0.8 in 2-D; 2015: 1,032 of 1,090 epidural and 990 of 1,052 facet-joint images classified, leave-one-out accuracy 94 percent epidural and 90 facet, features in 20 ms an image | SLIDE names the interspace from a sacrum class as the probe moves up (inferred from the abstract), so it would inherit a lumbosacral transitional vertebra, and no abstract mentions one; laminae (2015) and epidural landmarks (2018) are detected to find a plane, never measured; private data, no code, abstracts only here

rows.row_markdown: Osiowski and others, lumbar rib meta-analysis (Surg Radiol Anat 2024;46(12):2057-2066, doi 10.1007/s00276-024-03504-9, PMC11579145, CC BY) [full] and Henry and others, cervical rib meta-analysis (World Neurosurg 2018;110:e965-e978, doi 10.1016/j.wneu.2017.11.148, PMID 29203316) [abstract] | Osiowski: 9 studies, 5,430 people, 141 lumbar ribs, only series of spines with normal segmentation and 17 thoracolumbar vertebrae that state counting the whole column; Henry: 141 studies, 77,924 participants | None | Lumbar rib pooled 2.1 percent (95 percent CI 1.0 to 4.6), CT 1.6 (0.6 to 4.3; 4 studies, 2,906), radiograph 2.1 (0.4 to 11.1; 3 studies, 2,100), bilateral 65.4 (39.4 to 84.6); I2 90.11 (CT) and 95.20 (radiograph), by region under 0.001 to 97.16; LFK index -4.55; random effects in MetaXL 5.3; cervical rib 1.1 percent in healthy people and 29.5 in thoracic outlet syndrome, more than half unilateral, no CI in the abstract | No pooled estimate was found for eleven or thirteen rib pairs (the reader's Europe PMC search, not rerun here); the lumbar-rib definition requires normal segmentation and 17 thoracolumbar vertebrae, so it excludes every spine with a count variant, the stratum a naming rule needs; neither tells a thirteenth rib from a lumbar rib by a stated length rule

rows.row_markdown: - Four more reader-counted series, none open (the bullet's Lodz 2026 is Jankowski 2026, PMC13703058): Forseen 2015 [abstract] (244 whole-spine CTs: lumbosacral transitional anatomy with eleven ribs in 5 of 7, thirteen 8 of 11, twelve 24 of 234, denominators summing to 252 against 244 and differing from its lowest-rib counts of 8, 11 and 225); Sun 2025 [full, PMC12630705, CC BY] (UK Biobank, 500 non-carriers chosen as controls, counted by hand down from C2 on aligned DXA and Dixon MRI, assuming 7 cervical and 12 thoracic: four lumbar 8, 1.6 percent, six lumbar 16, 3.2, eleven rib pairs 13, 2.6, L1 ribs 10, 2.0; the deep learning there only aligns DXA to MRI, code on GitHub, images by UK Biobank access); Duman 2026 [full, PMC13517915, CC BY] (517 thoracic CTs, one radiologist: hypoplastic twelfth rib 55, 10.64 percent, absent twelfth 22, 4.26, lumbar rib 12, 2.32, cervical rib 7, 1.35, any 96, 18.57, women 23.33 against men 14.44, p 0.013; no count method given, data on request); Zhou 2023 [full, PMC10722060, CC BY-NC-ND] (6,097 whole-body PET/CT screened, 450, 7.4 percent by division, with 23 or 25 presacral vertebrae, 211 and 239, 56 of them with a thoracolumbar transitional vertebra, 29 and 27, excluded; counted from the cervical spine by one musculoskeletal radiologist of 3 years, Castellvi read on the transverse processes, no posterior element segmented or measured, PACS VR and MPR, inter-reader ICC over 0.8 but STA 0.639 to 0.875, no data statement). Zhou 2023 and Sun 2025 are already in SchwingNet's full-spine-corpora-with-reader-counted-variants.md, which this section cites.

facts.row: facets.md, "What the family's prior art settles", Settled bullet on the 510-vertebra study
facts.reason: Gupta shares held; Singer 1989 gradual totals 71.5, not 59.6 alone. PubMed 23915998
facts.fact: The 510-vertebra study is Gupta and others 2018 (Ann Int Med Dent Res 4(4):AT29-AT33), 30 adult male dry columns; its shares are gradual over T11-L1 in 46 percent of columns on the right and 30 on the left, over T10-L1 in 3.33 percent on both sides, and abrupt at T12-L1 in the rest, so near-equal on the right only (about 49 gradual to 51 abrupt; 33 to 67 on the left); the share depends on the definition and the material: Forseen 2015 found 93 percent abrupt on 244 CTs, Pal and Routal 1999 93 percent gradual on 44 dry columns, Singer 1989 71.5 percent gradual (59.6 over T10-11 to T12-L1) and 28.5 abrupt on 630 CT-imaged spines.

facts.row: facets.md, Gaps, bullet "The 510-vertebra thoracolumbar facet study (360 thoracic, 150 lumbar) was seen only in a search summary ..."

facts.fact: Identified through OpenAlex (doi 10.21276/aimdr.2018.4.4.at6) and the journal's issue page, and read in full from the journal's PDF (CC BY-NC), so this bullet can go; the paper's own abstract says the change was abrupt or gradual "in almost equal number of columns" while its text gives 46 and 30 percent gradual over T11-L1 by side.

facts.row: facets.md, Not settled bullet "No method names a level from a facet measure ..."
facts.reason: Abstract never says segments count from C2; only numbering must. OpenAlex 10.4172/2165-7939.1000222
facts.fact: One manual method tests it: Forseen 2015 (J Spine 4:222) read the facet transition on 244 whole-spine CTs as a T12 marker and found it at the 19th segment in 184 (75 percent), the 18th in 50 (20) and the 20th in 10 (4), against the lowest rib at the 19th in 225 (92 percent); it concludes the transition is not reliable and that numbering must count caudally from C2, the negative result a facet-based naming rule has to beat.

facts.row: README.md, The families table, Facets row, "Closest to naming levels" cell
facts.reason: No per-patient agreement with rib-defined T12 is printed; 75 versus 92 percent. OpenAlex record
facts.fact: Facet-based level naming has been tried by hand: Forseen 2015 on 244 whole-spine CTs, where the facet transition lay at the 19th segment in 75 percent against the lowest rib there in 92 percent, and the authors rejected it as a landmark; Singer 1988 and 1989 (214 and 630 CT-imaged spines) give the junction's transition and asymmetry shares, and Du Plessis 2022 (173 CTs) the facet angle of the thoracolumbar transitional vertebra itself, 136 +/- 23 deg between T12's 182.8 and L1's 112.3.

The VERIDAH paper (arXiv 2601.14066) says its CT masks are in-house annotations supervised by an expert of 24 years and describes no CT segmentation model, no posterior-element label and no Dice.

facts.fact: Searched on 2026-10-30: no automatic cervical or lumbar rib detector was found (Europe PMC, 48 hits, 15 read; the nearest are Sun 2025's manual UK Biobank counts and Duman 2026's manual CT series); ultrasound lamina and transverse-process detection for anaesthesia is SLIDE, Pesteie 2015 and 2018, Chen 2026 and the public Cavalcanti 2025 set (rows above); no automated Castellvi typing was found on Europe PMC, OpenAlex or one web search, and Kwak 2025 states no prior study focused on automated LSTV classification; no SPINEPS CT paper was found (OpenAlex, the README's citations); the VerSe-based substructure work found outputs no measure of this family (Paccini 2023 partitions body, arch and processes; Marzola 2026, doi 10.1007/s12008-026-02639-w, abstract only, measures the dens of C2 with a model built on 25 VerSe C2 vertebrae and tested on 10); Zhou 2023 and VERIDAH segment and measure no posterior element (VERIDAH's rater defines a thoracic vertebra by a true rib regardless of length and settles ambiguous cases by morphology such as facet orientation).

facts.row: posterior-elements.md, Not settled sentence "No method handles a thirteenth rib pair, an eleventh, or a transitional vertebra's transverse process"
facts.reason: Forseen abstract gives 8 at the 18th segment and 5 of 7 eleven-rib. OpenAlex record; PMC13703058
facts.fact: Still true of automatic methods; by hand, Jankowski 2026 measured lumbar transverse process lengths across 11, 12 and 13 rib-bearing patterns (L3 longest in 30.0, 76.7 and 69.2 percent by single process; ICC 0.88 for single-side lengths) and Forseen 2015 read the lowest rib and the facet transition on 244 CTs with 7 or 8 eleven-rib and 11 thirteen-rib spines (the abstract gives both counts for eleven), so reader-measured cues exist to score an automatic transverse_length against.

facts.row: counts-and-anomalies.md, section 2 table, VERIDAH row ("a thoracic vertebra is defined by a true rib")
facts.reason: "true rib, regardless of the rib's length"; 16 cases (0.25%). https://arxiv.org/html/2601.14066v1
facts.fact: The rib is read by the human rater, not by the model: the paper defines a thoracic vertebra as one having a true rib regardless of its length, settles ambiguous cases by morphology such as facet orientation, and adapts Konin's rule at the lumbosacral junction so that a vertebra with any Castellvi anomaly is a sacralised lumbar vertebra regardless of type; SPINEPS was trained for that distinction on the MRI data and hand-corrected in 16 cases (0.25 percent); the CT masks are in-house annotations supervised by an expert of 24 years, no CT segmentation model is described, no Dice is reported, and no licence is stated for the weights.
